props.title: The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse
props.initialSlug: Wealth and war divide an Argentinian family in WWI

sections.content: The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse launched Rudolph Valentino into superstardom and stands as one of the highest-grossing silent films ever made. Metro Pictures poured an unprecedented $1 million into this epic adaptation of Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's novel about two branches of a family split by World War I. The film's massive battle sequences influenced later war epics like Wings (1927) and All Quiet on the Western Front (1930). Director Rex Ingram's innovative use of symbolic imagery, particularly in the apocalyptic vision sequences, established new possibilities for visual storytelling in cinema.

sections.content: Valentino's performance as Julio Desnoyers marked a seismic shift in male screen presence. His tango scene electrified audiences and established Latin lovers as a dominant archetype in Hollywood. This influenced countless subsequent stars including Blood and Sand (1922) and created the template for romantic leading men that persists today. The film's enormous success also helped legitimize feature-length dramatic films when many still saw cinema as mere entertainment.

The apocalyptic vision sequences, where the Four Horsemen emerge from the clouds, represented unprecedented special effects achievement for 1921. These scenes influenced fantasy elements in films like The Thief of Bagdad (1924) and Metropolis (1927). The blending of Biblical imagery with modern warfare created a template for epic storytelling that directors like Cecil B. DeMille would later expand upon in films like The Ten Commandments (1923). sections.content: The film's depiction of World War I set new standards for realism in combat sequences. Using thousands of extras and real military equipment, Ingram created battle scenes of unprecedented scale. This approach influenced war films for decades, from What Price Glory? (1926) to Hell's Angels (1930). The personal drama amidst historical conflict became a template for later classics like Gone with the Wind (1939).
